Chapter 8: The Land Ethic—Expanding the Circle of Care
There’s a quiet revolution happening in how some of us think about right and wrong. For so long, our sense of ethics has focused on relationships between people—how we treat our neighbors, strangers, even those who’ll come after us.
But what if we could stretch that circle of care even wider? What if it could include the land itself?
Picture this: a rancher out walking his fenceline at dusk. He stops, watching a coyote slip silently through the grass. In the old days, he might’ve seen that coyote as nothing but trouble—a threat to be chased off or worse.
But now, something’s different. He starts to wonder about the coyote’s place in the world—what does it eat, where does it sleep, how does it fit into the bigger story of life on the prairie? Suddenly, the coyote isn’t just an enemy. It’s a neighbor, maybe even deserving of a little respect.
Or think about this: in a busy city, a group of volunteers gathers to plant trees along a crowded street. The digging is tough, and it’ll take years for those trees to really make a difference. But as time goes on, the sidewalk grows shady, the air a little cooler, and those volunteers start to see themselves differently. They’re not just planting trees—they’re looking after the whole community. People, animals, soil, water—everything’s connected.
That shift in thinking—that’s what we call the land ethic. It’s about seeing ourselves as part of a much bigger community, one that includes not just people, but every living thing around us.
And it’s not really about following a strict set of rules. Instead, it’s about relationships. It’s about learning how to live in ways that honor the needs of the whole.
Now, let’s be honest—most folks find this idea pretty challenging. It goes against a lot of what we’re taught about individualism and ownership. But for those who give it a try, there’s something special waiting—a new sense of belonging, a feeling that you’re part of something bigger, and maybe even more lasting.
The land ethic isn’t some final destination you arrive at. It’s a journey. It keeps growing and changing, shaped by what we learn and by the world itself.
In the end, it’s a call to humility, to curiosity, and to care. And if you answer that call, you’ll find that not only do you change—the world around you starts to change too.
